name: Cloud Nine
anchor: No site was ever proposed. Marker is the Whitney Museum, New York, which showed the photocollage in a Fuller retrospective.
story: Around 1960 the architect Buckminster Fuller and his partner Shoji Sadao made a photocollage called Project for Floating Cloud Structures, known as Cloud Nine. It showed communities of several thousand people living inside enclosed geodesic spheres a mile wide, drifting above the ground. Fuller's reasoning was geometric. A geodesic sphere is built from triangles, and its shell area grows more slowly than the volume of air it holds, so at a mile across the structure weighs little compared with the air inside. He suggested that warming that air by one degree would lift the whole sphere. A sheet of polyethylene would cover the frame. Such a sphere could be tethered, left to float, or steered to follow the weather or to serve as emergency shelter. Nothing was built and no government was consulted, so no regulator ever ruled on it. The law it would have met is the 1944 Chicago Convention, under which each country has full control of the air above its land. A 2023 Leiden Law School analysis treats even a high-altitude balloon as an aircraft under that treaty, which suggests a drifting city would need permission from each country below it.
mechanism: A habitat that floats inside the atmosphere stays inside national airspace, so it gains no distance from state jurisdiction by leaving the ground.

name: JP Aerospace Dark Sky Station
anchor: Black Rock Desert, Nevada, where the Tandem airship test was flown in October 2011.
cost: About $500,000 to build the 175-foot Ascender test airship, per a US Air Force officer in 2004
story: JP Aerospace is a volunteer American group founded by the engineer John Powell, who has worked on high-altitude balloons and rockets since 1979. Its plan, called Airship to Orbit, has three stages. Sturdy airships carry people and cargo from the ground to a permanently inhabited floating base called a Dark Sky Station. Lighter craft built for thin air then climb from the base to orbit. The Register described the stations as mile-wide platforms at 140,000 feet, carrying telecoms equipment and tourist hotels. Powell told MSNBC in 2004 that the full-size station in his plan was two miles across. Real hardware exists at small scale. For the US Air Force it built a 175-foot V-shaped airship called Ascender at a cost of about $500,000. On 22 October 2011 an uncrewed craft called Tandem manoeuvred under power at 95,085 feet above Nevada, and a small prototype station has flown using helium balloons and carbon-fibre trusses. Nobody has lived on any of it. The group has made no claim to sovereignty. At 140,000 feet, about 43 kilometres, a station would sit well below both the 100-kilometre and 80-kilometre lines proposed as the edge of space.
mechanism: A permanently inhabited platform at 43 kilometres would remain below every boundary of space under discussion, so it would be subject to the airspace of whichever country lay beneath.

name: United States v. Causby
anchor: Land near the airport outside Greensboro, North Carolina.
stopped_by: US Supreme Court, which rejected ownership of the sky above land
laws: US Fifth Amendment; Air Commerce Act 1926; Civil Aeronautics Act 1938
challenge: The ownership theory lost; the landowners kept a narrower claim for low flights over their land
story: The Causbys owned 2.8 acres near an airport outside Greensboro, North Carolina, with a house and buildings used mainly for raising chickens. The end of a runway lay 2,220 feet from their barn. American military bombers, transports and fighters used the airport, and their low, frequent flights passed over the land. The family argued that this took their property, which under the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment requires payment. The Court of Claims agreed there had been a taking. When the Supreme Court heard the case in 1946 it had to address an old common-law rule, written in Latin as cujus est solum ejus est usque ad coelum, meaning that whoever owns the soil owns everything up to the sky. The Court wrote that this doctrine has no place in the modern world and that the air is a public highway, as Congress had declared. Otherwise every transcontinental flight would expose its operator to countless trespass suits. So a private landowner could not claim the sky as territory, though flights low enough to interfere with the use of the land could still count as a taking.
mechanism: Private ownership of land does not extend indefinitely upward, so a landholder cannot found a private domain on the air above their property.

name: Chicago Convention on International Civil Aviation
anchor: Chicago, Illinois, where the treaty was signed.
laws: Article 1 gives each state complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory
recognition: Treaty in force since 1947; parent of the UN's civil aviation agency ICAO
story: On 7 December 1944, 52 states signed this treaty in Chicago. It came into force on 4 April 1947, the same day the International Civil Aviation Organization began work. Article 1 says every state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over the airspace above its territory. The rule continues the 1919 Paris Convention on aerial navigation, and scholars trace both to the old Roman-law saying that whoever owns the soil owns up to the sky. The treaty works sideways as well as upward. Under the 1982 law of the sea treaty, a state's airspace also covers the air above its territorial waters. Beyond that limit, over the high seas, the convention says the rules in force are those set under the convention itself. What the treaty leaves out is the top. It never says how high sovereignty goes, and no later agreement has settled the height. This gap is why balloon flights, space planes and proposals for floating cities keep raising the same question. Any attempt at a self-governing place in the air above a state's land or territorial sea has to start from this text.
mechanism: Airspace is an extension of territory, so the air above a state's land or territorial sea already belongs to that state and cannot host a new sovereign without its consent.

name: Tokyo Convention and the flag of an aircraft
aka: Convention on Offences and Certain Other Acts Committed on Board Aircraft
anchor: Tokyo, Japan, where the convention was concluded.
laws: State of registration may exercise jurisdiction over offences on board; commander may restrain and disembark offenders
story: Signed in Tokyo on 14 September 1963, this treaty settled which country's law applies inside an aircraft in flight, including over the high seas or any other area outside every state's territory. It excludes state aircraft used for military, customs or police work. The state of registration, meaning the country where the aircraft is listed, is competent to exercise jurisdiction over offences committed on board, and each party must take the steps needed to establish that power. A commander, the crew and in some cases passengers may act to prevent offences, and the commander may put an offender off the plane or hand them to authorities when it lands. Other countries keep some rights. A state that is not the state of registration may not interfere with an aircraft in flight to exercise its criminal jurisdiction, subject to exceptions. The result resembles the flag rule for ships. An article in India's NLIU Law Review describes jurisdiction as primarily vested in the state of registry, with other states holding concurrent powers. An aircraft that flies over nobody's territory therefore still carries a national legal system with it, and a registered flying platform would too.
mechanism: Registration attaches a national legal system to an aircraft even over places no state owns, which leaves no gap in jurisdiction for an aircraft to exploit.

name: Air defense identification zones over the high seas
anchor: East China Sea, covered by China's 2013 zone. The first US zones of 1950 surrounded North America.
founder: United States (first zone, 27 December 1950); about 20 countries and regions since
laws: Unilateral national rules; reporting duties on aircraft
challenge: Contested by Japan and the United States in 2013; China's zone remains declared
story: An air defense identification zone is an area of non-territorial airspace in which a state, by its own declaration, requires aircraft to identify themselves and report. The United States created the first on 27 December 1950, shortly after President Truman declared a national emergency during the Korean War. It wanted early warning of a Soviet air attack. About 20 countries and regions now have zones, including Canada, India, Japan, Australia and the United Kingdom. Under US policy the zone applies only to commercial aircraft intending to enter US airspace. On 23 November 2013 China declared a zone over the East China Sea, with reporting obligations on aircraft as far as 300 miles from its territorial waters and over islands Japan controls. Tokyo warned of unpredictable events. South Korea then expanded its own zone so that it partly overlapped those of China and Japan. Legal writers disagree about the practice. One view holds that unilateral declarations break no law. Another says they conflict with freedom of navigation in international airspace. Robert Beckman's 2014 slides note that global conventions do not expressly prohibit them. No treaty authorises them either, so the zones rest on what other states tolerate.
mechanism: A state can extend practical control over open-ocean air through reporting rules without claiming sovereignty, and the lawfulness of that step remains disputed.

name: Chinese high-altitude balloon shot down off South Carolina
anchor: US territorial waters just off the South Carolina coast, where the balloon was shot down.
stopped_by: United States Air Force F-22 fighters
laws: Chicago Convention Articles 1, 3 and 3 bis applied by commentators
challenge: Shot down on 4 February 2023; debris recovered from the Atlantic
story: On 4 February 2023 US F-22 jets fired a missile at a Chinese high-altitude balloon. According to US military officials, it was then between 60,000 and 65,000 feet above US territorial waters off South Carolina. Beijing called this unlawful force against a civil aircraft. Washington said the balloon was a military surveillance craft violating its sovereignty. A Leiden Law School analysis worked through the legal options. A balloon counts as an aircraft under the 1944 Chicago Convention, and flying over US territorial waters without permission breached US sovereignty under Article 1, because at that height it was in airspace and not outer space. If it was a civil aircraft, Article 3 bis and customary law restrict the use of weapons. If it was a state aircraft, the convention does not apply and the general law on countermeasures does. A Jakarta Post article noted that the International Telecommunication Union treats stations at 20 to 50 kilometres as high-altitude platforms, while no treaty sets where airspace ends. The episode showed a country asserting its sovereignty with a missile at about 20 kilometres, around the altitude where Loon's internet balloons operated by consent.
mechanism: A state will use force to defend its sovereignty in the stratosphere, which confirms that the lower stratosphere is treated as national airspace in practice.

name: The undefined edge of space
anchor: Lausanne, Switzerland, seat of the air sports federation FAI that uses the 100-kilometre line.
founder: No founder; a standing dispute among states, agencies and scientists
laws: No treaty defines the boundary
recognition: No boundary is agreed in international law
story: Airspace belongs to the country below. Outer space belongs to no country. No treaty says where one becomes the other. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 and the Chicago Convention of 1944 are both silent on the height. The figure most often used is the Karman line at 100 kilometres, which the record-keeping body FAI uses to separate aeronautics from astronautics. Others differ. The US armed forces treat anyone who has flown above 50 miles, about 80 kilometres, as an astronaut, and NASA changed from the 100-kilometre figure to match them in 2005. In 2018 the astronomer Jonathan McDowell published a paper in Acta Astronautica proposing 80 kilometres as better suited to the physics and to the orbits actually flown. Another proposal sets the boundary at the lowest point a satellite can reach in orbit, with no fixed number. Legal writers describe two camps. The spatial camp wants a fixed height. The functional camp would classify an object by what it does. For anyone trying to set up a place beyond national control, the disagreement matters because the answer decides which body of law applies between roughly 20 and 100 kilometres up.
mechanism: The lack of a legal boundary leaves the band between the highest aircraft and the lowest satellites open to competing claims and to no settled regime.

name: Loon
anchor: Winnemucca, Nevada, a Loon launch site; service was aimed at Kenya.
stopped_by: Alphabet, which ended the company in 2021 because it lacked a viable business
laws: Country-by-country flight approvals
challenge: Never challenged; it asked permission from each state
recognition: Approved by Kenya (2020); overflight deal with Uganda (2019 Reuters report)
story: Loon floated balloons carrying mobile network equipment about 20 kilometres up, steering them on stratospheric winds to give internet access to remote areas. Development began in 2011 at Google X, and it later became a separate company under Google's parent, Alphabet. Earlier service reached Sri Lanka in 2015 and Puerto Rico in 2017 after Hurricane Maria. Its Kenyan rollout shows how the law worked at that height. Loon signed a contract with Telkom Kenya in July 2018. It then waited until March 2020 for the Kenyan government's formal approval for balloons to operate in the stratosphere above the country. Because balloons drift, Loon also signed an airspace agreement with neighbouring Uganda. A company spokesperson told Reuters the balloons might get above the Ugandan stratosphere while serving Kenya. Launches took place in the United States, with balloons navigating across to Africa. In January 2021 Alphabet announced Loon's end, and Hackaday's account points to weak finances and a business model that served poor areas without enough income. Loon is useful as a precedent for what it never did. At 20 kilometres, with US corporate backing and no people on board, it still sought consent from each country along its path.
mechanism: Loon treated the stratosphere as national airspace by obtaining approval from each state whose territory its balloons might drift over, even at 20 kilometres.

name: Asgardia
anchor: Administrative centre in Vienna, Austria. Its only territory, the Asgardia-1 satellite, was launched from Virginia.
pop: Nobody has lived there. About 290,000 registered online citizens claimed in March 2019
currency: Solar (planned crypto-currency, named in the constitution) and Lunar (reserve unit)
laws: Constitution adopted 18 June 2017; 150-seat parliament; four-panel court under a Supreme Justice
challenge: Never tested. Its satellite stayed under US jurisdiction
recognition: None; no state or UN recognition
cost: NanoRacks said similar satellite projects cost about $700,000; actual cost undisclosed
story: On 12 October 2016, at a Paris press conference, the Russian engineer Igor Ashurbeyli announced a new space nation. Over 100,000 people applied online within two days and 500,000 within three weeks, though tougher checks cut the figure to about 210,000 by June 2017. A constitution passed that month, with no formal way to vote no, and made the state a kingdom. On 12 November 2017 an Antares rocket carried Asgardia-1, a two-unit CubeSat of 2.8 kilograms and 512 gigabytes, to orbit. It entered service on 6 December. Asgardia called itself the first nation with all its territory in space. Legal scholars disagreed, because US companies launched it on a NASA-funded mission and it stayed under US jurisdiction. The Outer Space Treaty bars states from claiming space and holds the launching state responsible. Parliament met in Vienna, and Ashurbeyli was inaugurated at the Hofburg palace on 25 June 2018. He won re-election with 93.17 percent in September 2022. Asgardia-1 re-entered the atmosphere on 12 September 2022, and no successor satellite turned up in this research. The most recent verified activity dates from December 2022 and 2023, in a magazine Ashurbeyli edits, so its activity in 2026 is unconfirmed.
mechanism: A satellite launched and registered through another country gives its owners no territory, because Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty keeps jurisdiction with the registering state.

name: Bogotá Declaration
aka: Declaration of the First Meeting of Equatorial Countries
anchor: Bogotá, Colombia, where the eight states met and signed.
founder: Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Congo, Zaire, Uganda, Kenya and Indonesia
stopped_by: Lack of international support; the claims were largely abandoned
laws: Declaration only
challenge: Rejected in practice; it never won wider support
story: On 3 December 1976, at the end of a meeting in Bogotá, eight countries on the equator signed a claim to part of space. They were Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Congo, Zaire, Uganda, Kenya and Indonesia. A geostationary orbit is the ring about 36,000 kilometres above the equator where a satellite seems to stay fixed over one spot, which makes it valuable for communications. The declaration called this orbit a scarce natural resource and said the segments above each signatory's territory fell under its national sovereignty. Segments over the high seas were to be the common heritage of mankind, governed by all nations together. The states dealt with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans national claims in space, by arguing that the treaty had never defined outer space and so did not cover the orbit above their land. Many of the signatories were newly independent and resented a rule set by states that already had satellites. The claim drew little support elsewhere and was later largely abandoned. It remains one of the few attempts by governments to challenge the treaty's central rule, and the only one aimed at a physical band of orbit.
mechanism: Equatorial states tested whether the undefined edge of space could let territorial sovereignty reach geostationary orbit, and other states' refusal left the Outer Space Treaty rule standing.

name: Tongasat
anchor: Nuku'alofa, Tonga, seat of the Supreme Court that ruled on the company.
founder: Nilson, with Princess Salote Pilolevu Tuita and King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV
stopped_by: Tonga's Supreme Court, on the Chinese grant money (2018); an appeal was rejected in 2019
laws: Agency agreement with the Kingdom of Tonga; ITU filings
challenge: Lost in Tonga's Supreme Court over more than $46 million in public money
recognition: ITU filings accepted; many operators and governments objected
cost: Slots to be leased at $2 million a year each; over $46 million in Chinese grant aid was paid to the company
story: The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) assigns places in geostationary orbit to countries that file for them. In 1987 a man named Nilson persuaded Tonga's king, through Princess Pilolevu, that a tiny state could file too. The government acted in April 1988. On 23 March 1990 Nilson applied for sixteen of the last useful slots, out of 180. Intelsat and the United States objected, and critics called it a money scheme. The plan was to lease each spot for $2 million a year, with half the profit going to the government. Rimsat licensed slots in 1992 and flew satellites, and Nilson was fired in February 1994 after an audit found he owned Rimsat shares. Wikipedia calls the arrangement in effect a flag of convenience for space. To stop slots expiring, the company bought an aging satellite from 1981 and moved it to 70 degrees East. China later wanted 130 degrees East, and Tonga gave way in exchange for grant aid, part of which went to Tongasat. On 17 August 2018 Lord Chief Justice Paulsen ruled that the company had unlawfully received over $46 million in public money. Tonga's Supreme Court rejected its appeal in April 2019.
mechanism: ITU rules let any state, however small, file for orbital slots and rent them to foreign operators, which turned national filing rights into a saleable commodity.

name: MirCorp
anchor: Amsterdam, where MirCorp was based. The station was in low Earth orbit.
founder: Walt Anderson, Jeffrey Manber and RSC Energia
stopped_by: Lack of funds, NASA opposition, and the deorbiting of Mir in March 2001
laws: Commercial rights granted by RSC Energia; Russian station
challenge: Lost: NASA pressed for deorbit and US export licences were delayed
recognition: RSC Energia authorised it; NASA objected
cost: Commercial use priced at $10 million to $20 million; Manber said the company failed for about $10 million
story: MirCorp tried to turn the aging Russian station Mir into a private business. Amsterdam-based MirCorp got authorisation from the Russian company RSC Energia, a shareholder, to lease Mir for tourism, advertising, industry and science for the rest of its life. Its chairman, the American telecoms millionaire Walt Anderson, was thought to be the main source of the first money, and its president was Jeffrey Manber. NASA administrator Dan Goldin said he was not pleased, because the plan drew Russian attention and funds from the International Space Station. On 4 April 2000 MirCorp funded Soyuz TM-30, which carried Sergei Zalyotin and Aleksandr Kaleri to reactivate and repair the station. It was the last crew Mir ever received. The company signed up Dennis Tito as a paying passenger and said it had a business backlog of $100 million, including a planned reality show. Money ran out when the dot-com crash hit Anderson's investments, and State Department export approval arrived too late. Mir was deorbited in March 2001. Tito flew to the International Space Station instead that year. Anderson later pleaded guilty to tax evasion and received nine years in prison.
mechanism: A private company can rent operating rights on a state-registered station, but the station's jurisdiction, launches and export licences stay with governments that can end the venture.

name: International Space Station Intergovernmental Agreement
anchor: Paris, seat of the European Space Agency, which publishes the legal summary used here. Signing location not verified.
founder: United States, Canada, Japan, Russia and European Space Agency member states
pop: Rotating crew; 7 aboard on 4 November 2026 per SpaceOdysseyHub
laws: Article 5: national jurisdiction over registered modules and nationals. Article 22: criminal jurisdiction. Crew Code of Conduct, September 2000
story: The International Space Station has people living on it permanently and has no government of its own. A treaty signed on 29 January 1998 divides it. Under Article 5, each partner keeps jurisdiction and control over the modules it registers and over its own nationals on board. The European Space Agency describes this as treating those modules as part of the partners' territories, so that European law applies inside Europe's Columbus laboratory. National courts therefore hear cases on criminal matters, liability and intellectual property, with special rules for Europe under Article 21. Article 22 covers crime. A Congressional Research Service paper explains that each country may exercise criminal jurisdiction over its own nationals in any module. Where misconduct affects the life or safety of another country's national, or happens in or damages another partner's module, the suspect's country must consult the affected country. The affected country may prosecute if the suspect's country agrees or gives no assurance that it will prosecute. A Crew Code of Conduct agreed in September 2000 sets a chain of command. So a station built by many states produced a patchwork of national law, in which space hardware behaves like an extension of a registering country.
mechanism: The treaty shows that long-term habitation in orbit extends existing national jurisdiction module by module and creates no new self-governing territory.

name: Aurora Station
anchor: Houston, Texas, base of Orion Span.
stopped_by: The company itself; sources date the shutdown to March 2021 or 2022
cost: $9.5 million per person for a 12-day stay; $80,000 refundable deposit
story: In April 2018 the Houston startup Orion Span, led by former software engineer Frank Bunger, announced a hotel in orbit called Aurora Station. It was to be a single module 35 by 14 feet, about the interior volume of a Gulfstream G550 jet, orbiting 200 miles up. It would hold four guests and two crew. A 12-day stay would cost $9.5 million per person, and an $80,000 refundable deposit held a place. Launch was planned for late 2021, with guests the following year. The company said its chief architect and its operating and technical officers came from NASA, but it would not say how much money it needed. No launch contract was signed and construction never started. An archived copy of its website said in March 2021 that operations had stopped and deposits had been refunded, while a later radio report gave 2022 as the year it ceased. The project made no claim to sovereignty. It matters here as an early test of the business case for a private orbital place, and it failed on money before any regulator had to rule on who would govern guests on board.
mechanism: The venture ended on finance before any licensing or jurisdiction question arose, leaving private-hotel law in orbit untested.

name: Vast Haven-1
anchor: Long Beach, California, where Haven-1 is being integrated.
laws: None of its own; expected to operate under US law
story: Vast is an American company building Haven-1, which it calls the first commercial space station. It was announced in 2023 and is a single module of about 14 tons, as described by Universe Magazine. It has about 45 cubic metres of living space by Wikipedia's figures and depends on a docked SpaceX Crew Dragon for life support and power. Crews of four would stay for up to 30 days, though Payload reports missions of up to two weeks. In early 2026 Vast moved the launch from 2026 to no earlier than the first quarter of 2027 on a Falcon 9. Crewed flights depend on SpaceX agreeing that it is safe to dock. CEO Max Haot told Ars Technica that this could be two weeks after launch or any time in the station's three-year life. No report of a launch had appeared as of November 2026. Vast's larger Haven-2 is meant to keep crew on board continuously after the International Space Station retires. Vast makes no sovereign claim. Under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, the United States must authorise and supervise its private companies in space, so a private station would stay under a government's supervision.
mechanism: A wholly private station, under Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, still needs its home state's authorisation and continuing supervision, so private ownership does not bring independence.

name: Axiom Station, Orbital Reef and Starlab
anchor: NASA Johnson Space Center, Houston, which runs the procurement.
founder: Axiom Space; Blue Origin with Sierra Space and Boeing; Voyager Space with Airbus and Northrop Grumman
laws: NASA Space Act Agreements and contracts; US oversight
cost: $415.6 million in NASA Phase 1 awards in December 2021; later raised to $172 million for Orbital Reef and $217.5 million for Starlab
story: NASA plans to replace the International Space Station with privately owned stations it would rent. In December 2021 it gave three teams a total of $415.6 million under its Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program. Blue Origin's Orbital Reef, announced on 25 October 2021 with Boeing and Sierra Space, was later raised to $172 million. Starlab, from Voyager Space, was raised to $217.5 million after Northrop Grumman joined it. Axiom Space holds a fixed-price contract. Each has moved at a different pace. Axiom plans to attach its first module to the existing station and then fly free as early as 2028. Starlab, by then a Voyager and Airbus venture, is aiming for 2029. A National Space Society summary says Orbital Reef remains in various stages of planning. A second round was meant to pick winners by April 2026. NASA placed it on hold on 28 January 2026 to match revised requirements, and a corrected industry report from 24 September 2026 said no Phase 2 award had been made. All of them depend on a government as main customer and funder. None seeks to govern itself, and their legal template is the national jurisdiction used on the station they would replace.
mechanism: The private successors to the ISS are funded through US government agreements, so ownership moves to companies while authorisation and control remain with a state.

name: Bigelow Aerospace
anchor: North Las Vegas, Nevada, the company's base.
stopped_by: The company itself laid off all 88 employees in March 2020
pop: Nobody lived on its free-flying modules; ISS crews enter BEAM
laws: FAA payload review letter to Bigelow in 2014, cited by lawyers
cost: Robert Bigelow's own money: $250 million by 2013, with up to about $500 million pledged
story: Bigelow Aerospace, founded by Robert Bigelow in 1998, built inflatable space station modules from technology licensed from NASA in 2000, after Congress cancelled NASA's TransHab project. It came closer to private orbital habitats than any other company of its time. It flew two uncrewed free-flying prototypes in 2006 and 2007 and added an expandable module called BEAM to the International Space Station in 2016. By 2013 Bigelow had put in $250 million of his own money and said he was ready to spend up to about $500 million. The company also pushed regulators. Space lawyers at TechFreedom note that in a 2014 letter to Bigelow the Federal Aviation Administration insisted it could leverage its existing authority over such missions, which they criticised as having no clear limits. In March 2020 Bigelow laid off all 88 staff, blaming the COVID-19 pandemic. When its engineering contract with NASA ended, NASA took ownership of BEAM. The company is described as dormant and defunct as of January 2024.
mechanism: A private firm's habitat depended on US regulators and NASA contracts throughout, and when the contract ended the only module in use passed to a government agency.

name: The ORBIS lease proposal
anchor: Lubbock, Texas, home of Texas Tech University, where the author worked.
laws: A model private lease in place of state law
story: In 2019 Alexander W. Salter of Texas Tech University published "Settling the Final Frontier: The ORBIS Lease and the Possibilities of Proprietary Communities in Space" in the Journal of Air Law and Commerce, volume 84, starting at page 85. The article runs from page 85 to page 114. Salter starts from Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which forbids any state from extending territorial jurisdiction into outer space. If that rule stays, he argues, rules for human conduct in space must come from somewhere other than states. His answer is the proprietary community, meaning a settlement privately owned and operated, and he surveys the mechanisms that make such communities likely to supply good governance. He then looks at a model lease called ORBIS, drawn up by Spencer MacCallum, whom he describes as a famed scholar of proprietary communities. Salter argues that this voluntary model would be expected to outperform others. He also discusses the implications for state policy. No settlement is known to have used the lease, and it remains a paper proposal. Other commentators, including those writing on SpaceX, argue that Article VI still requires a state to authorise and supervise private actors in space.
mechanism: The paper proposes contract in place of sovereignty as the source of law in space, which reads the non-appropriation rule as leaving room for private governance.

name: Flags of convenience for spacecraft
anchor: Boston University, publisher of the Taghdiri note. Another discussion took place at UN COPUOS in Vienna in 2016.
founder: No founder; a predicted practice in commercial spaceflight
laws: Registration Convention; Outer Space Treaty Article VIII
story: Merchant ships can register in a country with light rules and fly its flag, which is called a flag of convenience. Lawyers have asked whether spacecraft can do the same. Adrian Taghdiri's 2013 note in the Boston University Journal of Science and Technology Law, written as space tourism was starting, predicted that some countries would set loose rules to attract private space companies. He warned of environmental harm, more debris and danger to passengers. Space law limits the effect but does not remove it. Under the Outer Space Treaty, a state on whose registry an object is carried keeps jurisdiction and control over it and its personnel. Any launching state, meaning one that launches or procures a launch, stays liable for damage. So a cheap registry cannot erase the liability of the country whose soil was used. A presentation at the UN space law subcommittee's 2016 symposium in Vienna set out the maritime concept and its reduced oversight, and asked how it fits space objects. The closest working example is in orbital slots. Wikipedia describes Tongasat's business as, in effect, a flag of convenience for space, and later filings came from Gibraltar, Papua New Guinea and Bermuda.
mechanism: Registration lets a company choose its regulator to a degree, while launching-state liability keeps at least one responsible state attached to every object.

name: Swarm Technologies and the unlicensed SpaceBEEs

challenge: Lost: paid $900,000 and accepted oversight

story: In April 2017 the American startup Swarm Technologies asked the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for an experimental license to run four very small CubeSats called SpaceBEEs and two ground stations. In December 2017 the FCC said no, over concerns about whether such small satellites could be tracked. Swarm launched them anyway on 12 January 2018, on a rocket from India. This looked like a way round American rules, since the launch was on foreign soil. The FCC found otherwise. Swarm was an American company, and its satellites had sent signals to ground stations in Georgia for more than a week. The agency also found unauthorised tests from weather balloons. In December 2018 Swarm signed a consent decree. It paid a $900,000 penalty to the US Treasury, accepted a strict compliance plan and agreed to file pre-launch reports for three years. The case shows how a nation reaches spacecraft even when it did not launch them. The hook was radio. A satellite needs spectrum to reach users on the ground, and a state controls who can transmit within its borders. Launching abroad did not free Swarm of its home country's regulators.
mechanism: Control of radio licences and ground stations gives a state practical jurisdiction over satellites launched from other countries.

story: Though orbit belongs to no country, a national telecoms regulator shapes what happens there. In a 2018 order, the Federal Communications Commission granted SpaceX authority for a system of 4,425 satellites offering broadband around the world. The order says the grant will enable SpaceX to bring service to users. The same agency has shown it can punish operators for what they leave in orbit. In 2002 Dish Network launched a satellite called EchoStar-7 into geostationary orbit. In 2012 it agreed to move it 186 miles above its station at end of life. In February 2022, low on fuel, it had managed only about 76 miles. On 2 October 2023 the FCC announced its first fine for space debris. Dish admitted liability, paid $150,000 and accepted a compliance plan. The terms of service for Starlink's 2020 beta test confirm the pattern on Earth, since service on Earth or the Moon was to be governed by California law. A company that wants customers on the ground therefore stays within reach of a regulator that licenses its signals.

name: Kessler syndrome and the physical limit on orbital territory
anchor: Houston area, NASA Johnson Space Center, used as a nominal anchor for NASA debris research; the phenomenon has no surface location.
founder: Donald J. Kessler and Burton G. Cour-Palais (authors of the 1978 paper)
laws: No treaty sets a debris limit; rules are national
story: Any plan to live or build in orbit faces a physical limit as well as a legal one. In June 1978 the NASA scientists Donald J. Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais published "Collision Frequency of Artificial Satellites: The Creation of a Debris Belt". They showed that if low Earth orbit became crowded enough, collisions would create debris that caused more collisions, in a chain. Kessler applied to satellite records a technique developed for studying the asteroid belt. He found that 42 percent of catalogued debris came from 19 events, mainly explosions of spent rocket stages. At the time many thought atmospheric drag would clear debris faster than it formed. By 2025 there were an estimated 11,800 satellites in orbit, of which 7,135 belonged to Starlink, and the cascade becomes likelier as that number grows. This limit bears on sovereignty. Orbit is shared by default. A settlement cannot fence off its orbit, and one state's or company's debris endangers every other occupant. The FCC's 2023 fine against Dish Network is an early case of a state enforcing debris rules, since no global regulator does so.
mechanism: Because debris crosses every orbit, activity in orbit cannot be physically separated, which limits how exclusive any claim to an orbital place can be.

story: SpaceBelt was an orbital version of a data haven, a place to keep information out of reach of national rules. Cloud Constellation Corporation of Los Angeles proposed to store customers' data on satellites in low Earth orbit and pass it between them, so that it never crossed the public internet or the land networks of any country. Its marketing said this would sidestep jurisdictional restrictions and laws on how data moves between countries. President Cliff Beek pitched the ability to host data without wrangling with international compliance laws, and in 2017 the company pointed to the coming European data protection rules, GDPR, as a sales reason. The trade press noted that those rules protect European residents' data even when it is processed outside the EU. The company raised $5 million in 2016. In December 2018 it announced a $100 million commitment from Hong Kong's HCH Group within a planned $200 million round, and it said it needed $480 million to reach orbit. In April 2020 it announced a benchmark test run with IBM on what it called Spacebelt hardware. No report of a launch, and no news after 2020, turned up in this research.
mechanism: The pitch assumed data stored in orbit escapes national law, although the Outer Space Treaty gives the launching and registering state jurisdiction over the satellite that holds it.

Two years later CNN reported that the hotel had a new name, Voyager Station, and a builder, Orbital Assembly Corporation, run by former pilot John Blincow, who also headed the Gateway Foundation. story: In 1980, going through a divorce and short of money, Dennis Hope read the Outer Space Treaty in a library. Article II bars nations from appropriating space, and Hope concluded this left individuals free. He filed a claim to the Moon, the other planets and their moons, sent it to the United Nations with a note saying he meant to subdivide and sell, and asked them to tell him if there was a legal problem. Hope says they never replied, and he treats the silence as approval. He went full time in 1995. Discover reported $9 million in sales to 4.25 million people at $19.99 an acre, and in a Vice interview he claimed 611 million lunar acres sold, plus plots on Mars, Venus, Io and Mercury. He says former US presidents own land through aides or gifts. In 2001 customers asked about their rights, so he wrote a constitution for a Galactic Government, ratified online in March 2004 by 173,562 votes. Ram Jakhu of McGill says the treaty was written to block such claims and no one can own property in outer space. His company website still sells deeds in 2026.
mechanism: Silence from the UN does not create title, and the Outer Space Treaty's ban is read by legal experts as blocking private claims along with state ones.

name: Nation of Celestial Space

story: James Thomas Mangan, an American public relations man and writer, issued a Declaration by the Nation of Celestial Space on 21 December 1948. On 1 January 1949 he registered a claim to all of outer space with the Recorder of Deeds and Titles of Cook County, Illinois. He said he acted for humanity, to stop any one country from dominating space. The nation claimed 19 members at its foundation and 19,057 a decade later, with another source giving 100,000. In 1949 he notified the United States, Soviet Union, United Kingdom and United Nations that Celestia had banned further atmospheric nuclear tests. When the space race began he sent letters of protest to the Soviet and American leaders about their flights crossing his territory, though he later waived this for satellite launches. In 1958 he applied to join the UN and raised his flag outside its New York headquarters. He issued stamps, gold and silver coins and passports, and sent passports to astronauts. Nobody with power answered him. The project is thought to have ended when he died in 1970. The claim predates the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. This account rests on Wikipedia, as no better accessible source could be opened.
mechanism: A county deed office recorded the paper, which shows that registration by a local clerk has no effect on who holds sovereignty.

name: Artemis Accords safety zones
anchor: Washington, DC, seat of NASA and the US Department of State. Earth anchor.
founder: United States, with Australia, Canada, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, the UAE and the UK
laws: Non-binding principles made through bilateral arrangements; safety zones, heritage, debris
challenge: A McGill paper says they are often seen to conflict with the Moon Agreement; no legal test
story: The Artemis Accords are a set of non-binding principles for civil activity on the Moon and beyond, set up by NASA and the US State Department. Eight countries signed on 13 October 2020: Australia, Canada, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States. According to NASA's own page, Vietnam became the 78th signatory on 28 October 2026. The most debated part is the safety zone. Signatories say they will give notice of where they are working and coordinate to avoid harmful interference. A zone's size and length reflect the work done there, and it ends when the operation ceases. NASA says the zones respect free access under the Outer Space Treaty. The Accords also say extracting space resources is possible before any further international rules exist, which a McGill University paper reads as differing from the Moon Agreement's call for an international regime first. Saudi Arabia signed the Accords on 14 July 2022 and notified its withdrawal from the Moon Agreement six months later. The China-Russia lunar base project has been described as a rival to the US-led Accords.
mechanism: Safety zones create a form of operational priority over a place on the Moon without calling it sovereignty, which tests how far use can go before it becomes appropriation.

The project was described as open to all interested countries. Talks with European agencies in 2021 ended after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. Chinese reports in 2023 said Russia, Pakistan, the United Arab Emirates and the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization had signed agreements and more than ten others were negotiating. Venezuela signed on 17 July 2023, which also gave China access to Venezuelan ground stations, and South Africa signed a memorandum on 1 September 2023. In 2023 China also announced a body called the International Lunar Research Station Cooperation Organization to coordinate the work. Construction is meant to start in 2031 and a permanent base to exist in the 2030s. In May 2025 a further memorandum set out plans to build a lunar power plant, with completion by 2036 according to Live Science. It is a planned base run by states under the Outer Space Treaty. name: Moon Agreement
aka: Agreement Governing the Activities of States on the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies
anchor: United Nations headquarters, New York, where it was adopted and is deposited. Earth anchor.
laws: Article 11: the Moon is the common heritage of mankind; states to set up an international regime for resources
challenge: Lost Saudi Arabia in January 2024; opposed by L5 Society campaigners in the US
recognition: 17 parties and 11 signatories per the UN treaty database
story: The UN General Assembly adopted this treaty on 5 December 1979. It opened for signature on 18 December 1979 and entered into force on 11 July 1984. Like the Outer Space Treaty, it says the Moon is not subject to national appropriation by any claim of sovereignty. It goes further in Article 11, which calls the Moon's resources the common heritage of mankind and commits parties to set up an international regime to govern exploitation when it is about to become feasible. The UN treaty database lists 17 parties and 11 signatories. No major space power has ratified. France, Guatemala, India and Romania signed without ratifying, and the parties include Australia, Austria, Belgium, Chile, Mexico, the Netherlands and Pakistan. Saudi Arabia acceded on 18 July 2012, then notified the UN on 5 January 2023 of its withdrawal, which took effect on 5 January 2024. That was six months after it signed the Artemis Accords. In the United States, campaigners from the L5 Society fought the treaty in 1979 and 1980, arguing that common heritage would stifle development and open space facilities to warrantless searches. The treaty is in force for its parties, and its resource regime has never been built.
mechanism: The only treaty to make the Moon's resources common heritage has few parties, and those that wish to mine have stayed out or left.

Gizmodo reported that it called itself Earth's leading lunar real-estate agency and sold deeds on its website for about $20 an acre. A GOOD magazine item described a stated mission of funding private settlement and of inhabiting the Moon permanently by 2015, with a moon atlas zoned for tourism, residential, scientific and commercial uses, and deeds copyrighted and deposited at the US Library of Congress. name: For All Moonkind
aka: Institute on Space Law and Ethics

laws: US One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act (2020); Artemis Accords section 9
recognition: Provisional observer status at UN COPUOS from December 2018
story: For All Moonkind is a nonprofit founded by Tim and Michelle Hanlon in 2017 to protect human heritage sites on the Moon, such as the Apollo landing sites and Neil Armstrong's bootprints. It asks a difficult legal question. The Outer Space Treaty forbids claiming the Moon, so no country can declare a protected park there in the way it can on its own land. The group worked around that in several ways. In December 2018 the UN General Assembly granted it provisional observer status. It helped US Senator Gary Peters draft the One Small Step to Protect Human Heritage in Space Act, which passed the Senate unanimously on 18 July 2019 and became law on 31 December 2020. The law applies only to companies working with NASA on lunar missions, which must agree to follow otherwise unenforceable NASA guidelines. Section 9 of the Artemis Accords, signed in October 2020, also commits signatories to preserve heritage sites. In March 2021 the group released a free registry of historic lunar landing sites, and in March 2023 it formed the Institute on Space Law and Ethics. It uses contract terms and shared promises because territorial protection is unavailable.
mechanism: Heritage on the Moon can be protected only through contracts and promises binding those involved, because territorial protection would be a prohibited claim.

name: Jenaro Gajardo Vera's title to the Moon

story: Jenaro Gajardo Vera was a Chilean lawyer, painter and poet born in 1919. On 25 September 1954 he went before the notary of Talca, César Jiménez Fuenzalida, and asked him to record his claim as owner of the Moon "from before 1857". That phrase was the legal formula Chileans then used to gain ownership of land that had no title deeds, a way of claiming long possession. The notary registered the deed, and it became well known in Chile, though Wikipedia's articles differ between 1953 and 1954 as the year of the claim, and the deed itself is dated 1954. The Chilean procedure was built for ordinary farmland with lost paperwork. Applied to the Moon, it shows that a working property system in one country has no way of checking whether a claimed object lies within its reach. It came 13 years before the Outer Space Treaty, so no international rule then spoke directly to it. Gajardo died at Santo Domingo, Chile, on 3 May 1998, and the retrieved sources show no state acting on the claim during his lifetime.
mechanism: A domestic notary can record a statement about the Moon, but national title procedures have no power over land outside the state's territory.

Lindsay's archapellago, misspelling and all. He left out the Earth, which he reasoned belonged to its inhabitants. He first excluded the Moon and Saturn, then claimed both in separate deeds. "On a May night in 1936," he later explained, he had looked at the full moon, thought of it as real estate and said to himself that nobody owned it. story: In 2016 the US had no agency clearly in charge of private missions beyond Earth orbit, though Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty requires a state to authorise and continually supervise its companies in space. Moon Express, a California company in the Google Lunar XPRIZE contest, wanted to land its coffee-table-sized MX-1E craft on the Moon. It asked the Federal Aviation Administration to review the payload. On 20 July 2016, announced on 3 August, the FAA gave a favorable payload determination, the first for a commercial payload meant to land on the Moon. It did so after consulting the State Department and NASA, and found no threat to safety, national security, foreign policy or treaty obligations, including Article IV. Lawyers at TechFreedom questioned whether a review letter met Article VI, since it requires authorisation and continuing supervision, and they urged Congress to create a clear statutory system. The company's founders talked about bringing metals and Moon rocks back to Earth. The retrieved sources do not show the mission flying, and the company's status in 2026 is unverified, so the status given here is an estimate.

story: Lonestar Data Holdings of Florida wants to run data centres on the Moon, and part of its pitch is legal. IEEE Spectrum reports that over 100 countries have laws restricting where certain data may be stored or processed, often within the country itself, and that the company offers space as a place beyond those lines, citing the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. A reader of the article called this exploiting a loophole in international law. Its first test unit, Freedom, flew on Intuitive Machines' Athena lander in the IM-2 mission. It carried data for the Florida state government and the Isle of Man, plus a game and a song. Athena landed on 6 March 2025, about 5 degrees from the south pole. It came down in a crater and on its side, about 250 metres or more from its target, and the mission ended after about 13 hours. Lonestar told FOX 13 that its payload was intact and the only surviving one. The lander belonged to an American company, and under Article VI of the treaty the United States answers for its companies' activities in space. Data held there would still sit in hardware tied to a state.

story: Virgiliu Pop, a Romanian space lawyer born in 1974, wrote the main history of private claims to the Moon. His book Unreal Estate: The Men Who Sold the Moon, reviewed in The Space Review in 2006, traces claims back 250 years to Prussia, where a king was said to have granted the Moon to a farmer with healing powers. That story surfaced only in the 1990s, when a descendant, Martin Juergens of Germany, contested Dennis Hope's claims. Wikipedia gives the date as 15 July 1756 and the king as Frederick the Great. Pop sorts claimants into groups, including those selling acres for money. In his final chapter he takes apart the Lunar Embassy's legal argument, and he says such claims are a trivial issue for space lawyers while having hijacked the public's view of space law. Pop reported that several million people held certificates of this kind. To make his point he himself claimed ownership of the Sun, a claim he argues is as bogus as the others. His doctoral thesis at the University of Glasgow was on landed property rights in outer space. Wikipedia's article on Celestia cites pages 25 to 40 of Unreal Estate as a reference.

name: Starlink's 'free planet' clause
anchor: California, whose law governs the same terms for Earth and Moon services. Earth anchor.
laws: Section 9 of Starlink beta terms: disputes on Mars to be settled by self-governing principles
challenge: No test; criticised by legal scholars
recognition: Nobody has recognised it; a contract cannot bind states
story: On 28 October 2020 SpaceX published terms of service for the Better Than Nothing beta of its Starlink internet service. Under the section on governing law, services on Earth or the Moon fell under California law. The next sentence read: "For Services provided on Mars, or in transit to Mars via Starship or other colonization spacecraft, the parties recognize Mars as a free planet and that no Earth-based government has authority or sovereignty over Martian activities." Disputes there would be settled by self-governing principles established in good faith at the time of settlement. Lawyers replied quickly. An article in the international law blog Volkerrechtsblog pointed to Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, under which the United States must authorise and supervise SpaceX's actions in space. It argued that SpaceX, though not itself bound by the treaty, cannot opt out, that its conduct in space is attributable to the United States, and that a claim like this one risks breaching Article II. A Richmond law journal note said the clause tried to sidestep international law. No one has yet reached Mars under these terms. Starlink's current terms could not be retrieved, so it is unconfirmed whether the clause remains in force in 2026.
mechanism: A private contract cannot release a company or its state from Outer Space Treaty duties, so the clause is an assertion and has no effect on international law.

story: Mars One, founded in 2012 in the Netherlands under Bas Lansdorp, planned a permanent colony on Mars with volunteers on a one-way trip, paid for partly by a reality television show. Accounts of the schedule vary between a first landing in 2023 and colonists in 2025, with robots by 2020, and by 2019 the target had slipped to 2031. New recruits would follow every 18 months. In 2013 some 202,586 people from about 140 countries applied within five months, paying a fee of nearly $40. The list was cut to 1,058 and then to 100. The company planned to raise about $6 billion. It was not an aerospace firm and meant to buy rockets, spacecraft, habitats and suits from outside suppliers, and critics said it looked like a scam, which it denied. A Swiss holding company bought the commercial arm, Mars One Ventures, in 2016. On 15 January 2019 the Civil Court of Basel declared Mars One Ventures bankrupt and thereby dissolved it, and an appeal failed. Its debts were about 1 million euros. Lansdorp said the Dutch nonprofit foundation was untouched, though the commercial arm was the part meant to raise money. No hardware was ever built, and no plan for Martian government was tested.
mechanism: The one-way colony ended under ordinary Swiss bankruptcy law long before it had to answer any question of space jurisdiction.

story: Robert Zubrin founded the Mars Society on 13 August 1998 at a convention in Boulder, Colorado, attended by 750 people. It is a volunteer American nonprofit, funded by donations, that lobbies for human missions to Mars. Its physical work has been on Earth. It runs analogue stations, simulated Mars bases, on Devon Island in the Canadian Arctic and at its Mars Desert Research Station, and crews there live under mission rules for weeks or months, including an 80-day stay in 2017. It has also asked how a Martian society would be organised. In 2019 it held a contest for a colony of 1,000, won by an MIT team with a design called Star City, split into five starting villages. In February 2020 it announced a second contest for a city state of one million people, with a $10,000 prize and proposals due by 30 June 2020. Zubrin's 2024 book The New World on Mars, as described by its publisher, predicts populous Martian city-states with a government of the people and inalienable rights that draw immigrants from Earth. No formal constitution adopted by the society could be verified. These are design exercises with no legal force.

name: Yemeni claim to Mars against NASA

laws: Claimed inheritance from ancient Himyaritic and Sabaean civilisations

story: In 1997, as NASA's Pathfinder mission and its small rover Sojourner were sending back more than 1,000 pictures from Mars, three men from Yemen filed suit against the American space agency for invading the planet. Adam Ismail, Mustafa Khalil and Abdullah al-Umari said they had inherited Mars from their ancestors 3,000 years earlier, and they based the claim on the mythologies of the Himyaritic and Sabaean civilisations of ancient Arabia. Their argument turned a familiar colonial question around, since they were cast as the rightful owners and an American state agency as the trespasser. The Outer Space Treaty had in any case barred national claims since 1967. The available sources are a popular history newsletter and Wikipedia. Neither gives a clear court record, so it is unknown which court heard it or how it formally ended. The case belongs on this map mainly because it is one of few claims to treat another planet as inherited land. It came four years before Gregory Nemitz sent NASA a bill for parking on the asteroid Eros.
mechanism: Ancestral inheritance was offered as a basis for title to a planet, a theory for which space law makes no allowance.

name: Gregory Nemitz's claim to asteroid Eros
anchor: Carson City, Nevada, Nemitz's home; the case began in federal court in Reno. Earth anchor.
stopped_by: NASA, the State Department and US federal courts
laws: Declaratory judgment suit under US law
challenge: Lost: dismissed; Nemitz appealed to the Ninth Circuit in July 2004 and the claim was dismissed by 2005

story: In March 2000 Gregory Nemitz, an aerospace consultant from Carson City, Nevada, published a claim to Asteroid 433 Eros. On 12 February 2001 NASA landed its NEAR Shoemaker probe there and left it. Nemitz sent NASA an invoice for $20, the parking and storage fee for the next century. NASA refused to pay, saying the Outer Space Treaty rules out private ownership of an asteroid. He then wrote to the State Department, which replied that in its view private ownership of an asteroid is precluded by Article II of the treaty. On 3 November 2003 Nemitz filed a complaint in federal court in Reno, asking it to decide whether the treaty rules out private ownership of asteroids. A court dismissed the suit. On 20 July 2004 he filed an appeal in the Ninth Circuit in San Francisco, arguing that the government's view left no room for private property in space. Futility Closet reports the claim being dismissed in 2005. Press and bloggers called this the first legal case on space property. It produced an official US government position against private title, which is unusually direct. His Eros Project website also promoted the idea of space property more broadly.
mechanism: The US State Department stated that Article II precludes private ownership of an asteroid, and the courts refused to give Nemitz title.

name: US Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act, Title IV
anchor: Washington, DC, seat of the US Congress. Earth anchor.
laws: 51 USC 51303: US citizens own resources they recover
challenge: Debated by scholars; no court test found
story: Signed on 25 November 2015, Title IV of this American law gives companies a right to what they mine. Section 51303 of Title 51 of the US Code says a US citizen engaged in commercial recovery of an asteroid resource or a space resource is entitled to any such resource obtained, including to possess, own, transport, use and sell it. It adds that this must comply with applicable law, including US international obligations. The drafting tries to avoid a conflict with Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, which says outer space and celestial bodies are not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, use, occupation or other means. Opinio Juris, a law blog, wrote that Congress did this by authorising private citizens and not the nation, by subjecting the right to international obligations, and by disclaiming extraterritorial sovereignty over any celestial body. The result separates the mineral from the ground it came from. A company could own a tonne of extracted ore while nobody owned the asteroid. Other countries have since copied the idea, as Luxembourg did in 2017. Whether one country can give rights that bind others remains debated, and no court decision on the question turned up in this research.
mechanism: US law grants ownership of extracted resources while disclaiming sovereignty over the body, which set the model of resource rights without land rights.

name: Luxembourg Space Resources Act
anchor: Luxembourg City. Earth anchor.
laws: Article 1 says space resources are capable of being owned; missions need authorisation
challenge: Doubted by Luxembourg's own Council of State; no court test
story: On 20 July 2017 Luxembourg adopted its Act on the Exploration and Use of Space Resources, the first such framework in Europe. Article 1 says that space resources are capable of being owned, and the rest of the law sets out authorisation and supervision for missions. It followed a program called SpaceResources.lu announced in 2016. At the time only the United States had a comparable law. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, binding on Luxembourg and then on 105 countries, was the obvious problem, and the Luxembourg Council of State itself noted that it was unclear whether international space law allows a country to grant property rights in resources extracted in space. The law sidesteps territory, since it concerns only the resources and says nothing of title to any part of the Moon or an asteroid. A small European state thus offered a legal base for space miners. The two best-known asteroid firms of that period, Planetary Resources and Deep Space Industries, were both sold by January 2019.
mechanism: A small state can offer a legal home to space miners by licensing them, which brings a shopping-for-jurisdiction dynamic to space resources.

name: UAE and Japan space resources laws
anchor: Tokyo, Japan; the UAE law comes from Abu Dhabi. Earth anchor.
laws: UAE Federal Law No. 12 of 2019; Japan Act No. 83 of 2021, Article 5 on ownership
challenge: No court test
story: After the United States and Luxembourg, two more countries legislated on space resources. In the United Arab Emirates, the Federal Law No. 12 of 2019 on the regulation of the space sector was issued by the president, passed by the Cabinet in late 2019 and had come into force by early 2020, according to a February 2020 Gulf News report. It covers licensing, registering objects, liability and insurance, and it also defines provisions on building facilities on other planets and on using space resources. Japan's parliament then passed the Act on the Promotion of Business Activities for Exploring and Developing Space Resources, Act No. 83 of 2021, which made Japan the fourth nation to do so. Article 5 of the official English translation is headed Acquisition of Ownership of Space Resources. According to Atalayar, the law lets Japanese companies access, find, exploit and obtain ownership of minerals from the surface and subsurface of the Moon, Mars or other bodies. Japan's own Hayabusa 2 mission had returned a few grams of dust from the asteroid Ryugu in December 2020, showing that extraction at a small scale can be done. Taken together with the American and Luxembourg laws, these acts form a growing group of states treating extraction as lawful use.
mechanism: Parallel national statutes are building state practice for ownership of extracted resources, without any multilateral treaty authorising it.

cost: Acquisition terms undisclosed
story: Two companies led the asteroid mining boom that pushed governments to write resource laws. Planetary Resources announced its plans in 2012, with prominent business backers. Nine months later Deep Space Industries, founded by entrepreneurs and space advocates, announced similar plans to prospect and extract resources such as water ice. Both built small spacecraft, and both benefited as the US passed its 2015 law and Luxembourg its 2017 one. Money ran out before mining began. A 2017 funding round for Planetary Resources with a major global mining company fell through, which led to large layoffs. At the end of October 2018 the blockchain firm ConsenSys bought it on undisclosed terms and identified only two of its people as staying. ConsenSys founder Joe Lubin said deep space capabilities fit a belief in Ethereum helping craft new rule systems for society. On 1 January 2019 Bradford Space announced that it had bought San Jose-based DSI, whose work by then was on small-satellite propulsion. Jeff Foust concluded in The Space Review that the answer to whether this was a boom or a bubble was clearly bubble. The laws they helped inspire remain on the books without their original customers.
mechanism: National resource statutes passed for these firms outlasted them, showing the law was written in advance of any actual extraction.

name: L5 Society and O'Neill's Lagrange colonies
anchor: Tucson, Arizona, home of founders Carolyn Meinel and Keith Henson. Earth anchor; L5 is a gravitationally stable point in space.
founder: Keith Henson and Carolyn Meinel, following Gerard K. O'Neill
stopped_by: Merged with the National Space Institute in 1987 to form the National Space Society
challenge: Won a political fight against US ratification of the Moon Treaty
story: In September 1974 Gerard O'Neill published "The Colonization of Space" in Physics Today, describing large settlements in space at stable points in the Earth-Moon system called Lagrange points. Keith Henson and Carolyn Meinel of Tucson read it and wrote to him. In August 1975 they incorporated the L5 Society, named for one such point. Its first four-page newsletter included a letter of support from presidential contender Morris Udall and said the long-range goal was to disband the Society in a mass meeting at L5. O'Neill's book The High Frontier came out in 1977. A NASA official of the day was quoted as saying a colony of 10,000 at L5 was feasible. No hardware was ever built, and critics put transport costs far too high for individuals to pay. The society's main achievement was political. With about 10,000 members and a phone tree, it fought the UN Moon Treaty in 1979 and 1980, arguing that common heritage rules would make space colonies impossible, and the US never ratified. In 1987 it merged with the National Space Institute to form the National Space Society, which still operates. Wikipedia says some members moved into 1980s missile defense work.
mechanism: A small advocacy group kept the United States out of the Moon Treaty, on the argument that settlements need sovereignty or property rights the treaty would deny.

story: Balaji Srinivasan, former chief technology officer of Coinbase, set out the idea in his 2022 book The Network State. An online community forms first, crowdfunds land in scattered places, and eventually seeks diplomatic recognition. In August 2024 he announced the Network School as a test, in a hotel at Forest City, a half-empty development in Johor, Malaysia. A 90-day trial took about 128 people, and a second phase from 1 March 2025 about 256. It became permanent in May 2025, with fees of about $1,500 to $3,000 a month. Malaysian officers inspected the site on 14 July 2026, after social media claims that Israelis had entered on second passports. They checked 266 foreigners from 40 countries and found all documents valid. Srinivasan suspended a planned $500 million investment. On 21 July the Iskandar Puteri City Council revoked the school's business licence, citing breach of licence conditions and premises use, and ordered it to stop from 22 July. Commentators also objected to its stated aims on sovereignty. Within hours Kazakhstan's digital ministry signed a memorandum to host a campus, with no city named at that point.
mechanism: A community that exists first online still needs a host state for its physical base, and that state's ordinary licensing power can end it.

name: Bitnation

passports: Blockchain ID cards for refugees, unrecognised

challenge: Vice reported it has no legal jurisdiction, since no state recognises it
recognition: None; it sought recognition as a sovereign entity
story: Susanne Tarkowski Tempelhof founded Bitnation in July 2014 as a voluntary nation. Citizens chose to join, and records of identity, marriage, birth and contracts would sit on a blockchain, a shared public ledger, in place of state registers. In 2015 it launched software for blockchain IDs and offered Bitcoin debit cards to refugees reaching Europe, a project called Refugee Emergency Response. Starting 1 December 2015 it offered a blockchain notary for Estonia's e-residents. Tempelhof told IBTimes her ultimate goal was recognition of Bitnation as a sovereign entity, which would create a precedent for an open source protocol to count as a jurisdiction. In 2017 it launched Pangea, with an arbitration token, and its refugee ID won a UNESCO prize. A Vice writer who joined in 2016 found about 25 volunteer embassies, including a German castle run as a bed and breakfast, and reported limited services and negligible interest. Since no state recognised it, it had no legal jurisdiction, and an asylum seeker could get little from an embassy. Tempelhof, whose father had been stateless, told Vice that Antarctica was the only place in the world not covered by nation-state jurisdiction. By August 2022 the domain had been sold and the project was considered defunct.
mechanism: A blockchain can record a marriage or an ID, but those records carry legal weight only where a recognised state chooses to accept them.

It had about 700 citizens from all five continents in 2009, according to its announcement in CoinNews. It sold real objects to give itself a physical presence. These included silver coins struck with its web address, stamps and a national identity card open to anyone over 18. A January 2010 post on the international law blog The View From LL2 described a Wirtland press release that proposed asking Nauru, the mined-out Pacific island nation, to transfer a piece of its territory. story: E-Residency is the reverse of the micronation model, since a real state issues a digital status to foreigners. Launched at the end of 2014, it lets foreign nationals set up and manage Estonian companies online without ever visiting the country. It gives a secure online identity. It does not make anyone a citizen or give the right to live there. The official dashboard says over 144,000 people from 187 countries have become e-residents and that they have founded or co-founded more than 43,600 Estonian companies. In 2025 e-residents set up a record 5,556 companies, 15 percent more than in 2024, and the state received nearly €125 million in direct revenue, including €54.5 million from labour taxes and €66 million from income tax in special cases such as dividends. The economy minister said every euro invested brought more than 12 back. Figures for the first seven months of 2026 show over 4,200 companies and 9,000 new e-residents. Bitnation tried to build on the program in 2015 with a blockchain notary. The system works without territory because it relies on Estonia's existing territory, law, courts and banks, so it extends a state's reach to people living elsewhere.
mechanism: An existing state can offer legal identity and company law to non-residents online, which provides the benefits cloud nations seek through a recognised sovereign.

laws: Bilateral agreement drawing on the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations
challenge: Not challenged
recognition: Bilateral agreement between two recognised states
story: In 2017 Estonia and Luxembourg signed an agreement that gives a government database a kind of embassy. Estonia wanted its state data to survive if its own territory was attacked or occupied. The kick-off took place in 2015. Under the deal, Estonian state servers sit in a high-security Tier 4 data centre in Luxembourg, under Estonian state control. Luxembourg's IT director Patrick Houtsch told NBC News that his government provided data centre services along with immunity. In June 2019 Estonia moved four core databases there, including land and business registries. The government describes it as something new under international law, an extension of the state in the cloud that takes account of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations but is not an embassy in the traditional sense. The arrangement shows how far a state can separate its records and functions from its land. Unlike a cloud nation, it starts from a recognised state and gets immunity by treaty with another recognised state. The registries could keep running if Estonia's own land were lost, a concern that Tuvalu's digital nation plan also addresses.
mechanism: Treaty-based immunity can place a state's core data abroad, separating some state functions from territory with a host state's consent.

story: A decentralised autonomous organisation, or DAO, is a group that makes decisions and holds money through software on a blockchain. It floated the idea of incorporating an actual city in Wyoming, if counties agreed, and putting deeds, titles, notaries and tax records on the blockchain. A reporter who drove out found the parcel after 20 minutes on back roads. No claim of independence turned up, and citizen here means a holder of the token. It first named the Mediterranean, then Greenland, then Uruguay. Founder Dryden Brown, who was homeschooled in California to pursue competitive surfing, said he had read Ayn Rand and the Austrian economists in high school. In 2022 he told a speechwriter the idea came from seeing looters in SoHo during the George Floyd protests. A New York Times report in December 2023 said he had raised $19.2 million, with Paradigm as largest backer and investors including Pronomos Capital and Balaji Srinivasan. The Times called him big on promises and light on specifics. A former employee told Mother Jones that Brown's ideal governance was authoritarian fascism without religion. story: Zuzalu was a temporary community run from 25 March to 25 May 2023 at the Lustica Bay resort in Montenegro, co-created by Ethereum's Vitalik Buterin. About 200 people stayed for the two months, with roughly 300 more visiting for a week or two. They were mainly longevity enthusiasts, cryptographers, AI researchers, entrepreneurs and followers of the network state idea. It tested something modest compared with a new country, namely whether people from an online community would live together for a short time. The model spread. By its third year, according to ForkLog, more than 30 pop-up cities had followed in places including Chiang Mai, Istanbul, Zanzibar, Ghana, Argentina, India, the United States and Berlin. Buterin broadly agrees with the Network State idea but worries that such projects could become clubs for the rich and put too much power in a founder's hands. He also argues that they must attend to the people living around them, and after floods in Chiang Mai the Zuzalu team took applications to rebuild homes. Each pop-up has operated as a guest in a host country under its ordinary law, so no question of sovereignty has come up. The 2023 event itself has ended; its offshoots continue.
mechanism: A pop-up city avoids any fight over sovereignty by staying a short-term guest under a host country's law, which leaves the question of self-government open.

name: World Service Authority and the World Passport
anchor: Washington, DC, office of the World Service Authority. Davis renounced his citizenship at the US embassy in Paris.

story: On 25 May 1948 Garry Davis, a former Broadway performer and American wartime bomber pilot, walked into the US embassy in Paris and renounced his citizenship. He said he was a citizen of the world. That November he stormed a session of the UN General Assembly in Paris. He founded the International Registry of World Citizens in 1949. On 4 September 1953 he declared the World Government of World Citizens, with the World Service Authority as its administrative arm, first in New York and later in Washington. It issued passports, identity cards and birth and marriage certificates. The New York Times wrote in his 2013 obituary that over 2.5 million documents had been issued and 950,000 people registered. Supporters said the papers helped refugees and stateless people. Detractors said he charged poor people for papers that are legally recognized almost nowhere. Foreign Policy reported over half a million passports sold, recognized by a small handful of countries, while the Authority claims 189 countries have at some time stamped one. Davis travelled for 65 years and was regularly arrested and expelled. Shortly before dying in July 2013 at age 91 in Vermont, he sent passports to Julian Assange and Edward Snowden.
mechanism: A document is a passport only if a border officer accepts it, so the World Passport works case by case on the discretion of each state.
