story: The Sovereign Order of Malta shows sovereignty continuing without land. It is a Roman Catholic order founded in Jerusalem in 1099, which at different times held land in today's Israel, Palestine, Cyprus, Greece, Italy and Malta. Napoleon took Malta in 1798, and the Congress of Vienna confirmed the loss in 1815. The seat moved through Trieste, Messina, Catania and Ferrara and reached Rome in 1834. Today it has its own government, laws, stamps and passports. It maintains diplomatic relations with 113 countries, up from 42 in 1981, and the UN General Assembly granted it observer status on 30 August 1994. Its two main properties in Rome, the Magistral Palace and the Magistral Villa, have extraterritorial status, like embassies, which the Order itself says is different from sovereign territory. The Order's own account says it is not a state, because it no longer has a territory or citizens, and that its sovereignty never depended on territory. So states recognise its sovereignty through long practice and diplomatic exchange. For anyone trying to build a digital nation it offers a precedent with limits, as its status rests on nine centuries of history and on recognition from states.
mechanism: International legal personality can exist without territory, but in this case it is built on centuries of history and bilateral recognition by states, which a new project lacks.

name: Nansen passport
anchor: Geneva, Switzerland, seat of the League of Nations.
founder: Fridtjof Nansen and the League of Nations
stopped_by: Superseded when the Nansen Office closed in 1938 and later UN refugee documents took over
pop: About 450,000 passport holders, in no place
laws: Intergovernmental arrangements from 1922
challenge: Recognised by states; won the 1938 Nobel Peace Prize
recognition: Internationally recognised through agreements among governments
story: In 1921 the Soviet government revoked the citizenship of Russians living abroad, including some 800,000 refugees from the civil war. These people could not cross a border legally, because they had no state to issue papers. In 1922 the League of Nations' High Commissioner for Refugees, the Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen, convened a conference in Geneva from 3 to 5 July 1922 that agreed a travel document, officially a stateless persons passport, which came to carry his name. In 1924 it was extended to Armenian refugees, and in 1928 to Assyrian, Bulgarian and Turkish ones. About 450,000 were provided. After Nansen died in 1930, the Nansen International Office for Refugees ran it in the League's name, and it won the 1938 Nobel Peace Prize, the year it closed. Later documents for stateless people and refugees come from national and international authorities. Unlike Garry Davis's later World Passport, this one worked for many, because governments had agreed to honour it. It shows that identity papers can exist with no country or territory behind them, and that acceptance depends on governments agreeing in advance. Holders of these documents still lived under the law of whichever state they had reached.
mechanism: An identity document can work without any territory behind it when states agree to honour it by treaty, which places its authority with those states.

name: Swedish Pirate Party hosting The Pirate Bay
anchor: Stockholm, Sweden, where the Pirate Party proposed hosting from parliament.
laws: Swedish parliamentary immunity was the proposed shield
challenge: The parliament plan depended on winning seats on 19 September 2010; TechRadar noted the party then had none
story: In 2010 the Swedish Pirate Party became the internet service provider for The Pirate Bay, a BitTorrent search site. Its founder Rick Falkvinge later wrote that this political step legally shielded the site, and that traceroutes in 2013 still showed its address ending at thepiratebay.piratpartiet.se. The party then went further. In July 2010 it proposed that, if elected to the Swedish parliament on 19 September 2010, it would host The Pirate Bay from inside the building. It argued that a rule protecting members of parliament would give total immunity for any political action in that working environment. The plan needed seats, and TechRadar pointed out that the party then had none. The party also offered to host WikiLeaks, and launched an anonymous internet provider. Falkvinge's site records a commenter noting that The Pirate Bay later moved to many places, including encrypted cloud services. The case sought cover inside a state's own legal protections. Sealand's data haven is covered elsewhere on the map.
mechanism: The Pirate Party tried to use parliamentary immunity in place of offshore distance, so a site's safe harbour would be built from a state's own law.

name: Tuvalu digital nation
anchor: Funafuti, Tuvalu.
pop: About 12,000 people in the physical country; the digital version has no residents
laws: Tuvalu's own law; seeks recognition of statehood despite land loss
challenge: Being tested by the question of land loss; no court ruling
recognition: Law Society Journal reports 26 countries recognised its digital statehood by December 2023
story: Tuvalu is a recognised Pacific country of about 12,000 people on low-lying islands that the UN Development Programme classes as extremely vulnerable to climate change. At the COP27 climate conference in November 2022 its Foreign Minister Simon Kofe, in a video, said that because the country was at risk it would move its land, ocean and culture to the cloud, in what it called the first digital nation. The plan is to map all 124 islands and islets, and to record cultural objects, language, elders' stories and dances, so that the diaspora and future generations can keep them if the land goes. Under the usual legal test for a state, territory is required, and nobody knows what happens when it disappears. So Tuvalu is seeking legal protection in advance. Australia's Law Society Journal reported that by December 2023, 26 countries, including New Zealand and Australia, had legally recognised its digital statehood, with a goal of 50. Australia also offered residency to 280 Tuvaluans a year. This is the only case on this map that runs in the other direction, in which an existing, recognised state plans for a future with no land.
mechanism: Tuvalu is testing whether a recognised state keeps its statehood after losing all land, by asking other states to commit to that recognition ahead of time.

name: A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace
anchor: Davos, Switzerland, where Barlow dated the text.
laws: None; it rejected government authority
story: On 8 February 1996, in Davos, John Perry Barlow, a founder of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, published a short text on the web aimed at the governments of the industrial world. It addressed them as weary giants of flesh and steel and said they had no sovereignty where its authors gathered. Written for a project called 24 Hours in Cyberspace, it set out in sixteen short paragraphs the argument that the United States lacked the consent of the governed to apply its laws to the internet, and that the internet lay outside any country's borders. The document created no institutions, members, courts or money, and it remains a statement of principle. Later events on this map ran against its claim. Swarm's fine, the licensing of Starlink and the Network School's lost licence all show that the physical parts of a network, its servers, satellites, ground stations and people, sit where governments can reach them. The text is still online at the Electronic Frontier Foundation.
mechanism: This text asserted that consent, as opposed to geography, should be the basis of authority online, which no state has accepted.

name: Embassies in Second Life
anchor: Malé, Maldives, the first country to open one.
recognition: Virtual embassies opened by recognised states
cost: Sweden's cost 400,000 kronor ($57,000)
story: In May 2007 recognised states began opening embassies in Second Life, an online 3D world. Sweden announced its plan in January and was to open on 30 May with a replica of the House of Sweden in Washington, built through the Swedish Institute for 400,000 kronor, about $57,000. The Maldives got there a few days earlier and put its own embassy on Diplomacy Island, a virtual diplomatic quarter. Foreign Minister Carl Bildt then opened Sweden's in a ceremony both in the world and in person. Estonia joined later in 2007, with Foreign Minister Urmas Paet citing the importance of the internet for communication and planning lectures and art shows. They are useful as a contrast. A real state entered a virtual world as a form of publicity and cultural outreach, and this added nothing to its legal status and created no territory. The current state of these embassies is unconfirmed.
mechanism: A recognised state's virtual presence is a communication tool that carries no territorial or diplomatic legal effect.

name: Dominion of Melchizedek
anchor: Taongi atoll, Marshall Islands, one of several places it claimed. It governs no place.
founder: Mark Pedley (also Branch Vinedresser, Tzemach Ben David Netzer Korem), possibly with his father David Pedley
currency: Claimed a currency listed on Bloomberg
passports: Sold for $10,000 at the time of a CBS report; on an EU list of fantasy passports
laws: Sold bank charters; claimed religious sovereignty
challenge: Described by the SEC as non-existent; condemned by the Marshall Islands
cost: $50,000 for a banking licence, $1,000 for an insurance company, per CBS; $47 million in one related insurance scheme
story: The Dominion of Melchizedek was declared in 1990 by Mark Pedley, also known as Tzemach Ben David Netzer Korem and Branch Vinedresser. CBS reported that he and his father had both served time for financial fraud. No one lives there. Over time it claimed the Colombian island of Malpelo, an invented submerged Karitane Shoal in the South Pacific, France's Clipperton Island, Taongi atoll in the Marshall Islands, and part of Antarctica. The Marshall Islands government condemned its claims. Its business was paper. It sold passports for $10,000, a banking licence for $50,000 and an insurance company for $1,000, along with government bonds. It said by the late 1990s that it had licensed some 300 banks. The Dallas Observer told of a former official awaiting sentence for his part in a scheme to peddle $47 million in bogus insurance policies. The US Securities and Exchange Commission described it as non-existent, and the Comptroller of the Currency as a non-recognised sovereignty. An EU list treats its passports as fantasy documents. Retired Comptroller official John Shockey spent ten years trying to close it down. It shows what a virtual country can be used for when buyers cannot easily check whether it exists.
mechanism: With no territory and no recognition, an entity can still cause real loss, because banks and buyers may not check sovereignty claims on paper charters.

name: Aerican Empire
anchor: Montreal, Canada, home of founder Eric Lis.
laws: Parliament under an Emperor, as a joke
recognition: None; a self-proclaimed monarchy founded for humor
story: The Aerican Empire is a self-proclaimed monarchy founded on 8 May 1987 by Eric Lis and friends in Canada. It began as a joke, with a name playing on the term American Empire. For its first ten years it was almost entirely fictional, claiming sovereignty over a vast galaxy of made-up planets and fighting wars with other micronations that never involved physical contact. Its mission statement says that the Empire exists to help society evolve to where the Empire itself is no longer needed. It describes a parliamentary system with elected bodies, under Lis as Emperor. It is included here since it represents the humorous and online end of the range and has lasted nearly 40 years. In 2025 it hosted the MicroCon 2025 gathering at a hotel in Montreal, attended by a reported 120 people from 48 micronations, though Wikipedia flags that report as needing a better source. No state has been asked to recognise it in any serious way. Its claim to imaginary planets is a parody of the more earnest claims elsewhere on this map, including those of Mangan and Hope.
mechanism: Parody states show that declaration alone has no legal effect, and they use that point for satire.

name: Kingdoms of Elgaland-Vargaland
anchor: Gothenburg, Sweden, where its biennial appearance was documented.
founder: Carl Michael von Hauswolff and Leif Elggren
laws: A founding constitution declaring a divine monarchic hierarchy
story: Elgaland-Vargaland was founded in 1992 by the artists Carl Michael von Hauswolff and Leif Elggren as a micronation in the form of a divine monarchic hierarchy. Its founding constitution claims sovereignty over places other countries leave out. Its physical territory is the border zones between all countries on Earth, plus areas up to 10 nautical miles wide lying outside the territorial waters of all countries. It also claims what it calls mental and perceptive territories, including the Hypnagogic State, the Escapistic Territory and the Virtual Room, the last of which it labels digital. The Gothenburg International Biennial for Contemporary Art documented the project. It is an artwork and it makes no serious legal demand, but its map of claims is exact. It points at spaces the international system treats as lines or gaps. It belongs in the digital zone because its founders listed a digital Virtual Room as claimed territory in the 1990s constitution, a few years before Barlow's declaration if the listing dates from the founding, which the biennial page implies without giving a separate date. Current activity beyond the biennial's record is unconfirmed.
mechanism: As art, it treats borders and virtual space as claimable territory, showing how far a declaration can be pushed when nobody is obliged to answer.

name: Kingdom of Talossa
anchor: Milwaukee, Wisconsin, where a teenager's bedroom was declared a kingdom.
pop: A teenager's bedroom at first; 157 active online citizens in August 2023
laws: Own government and a constructed language
story: On 26 December 1979 Robert Ben Madison, aged 14, declared his bedroom in Milwaukee a sovereign nation, the Kingdom of Talossa, with himself as King Robert I and sole resident. He picked the name after finding that it means "inside the house" in Finnish. Friends joined him. They made a government, a flag, a handwritten newsletter and a language, which by Madison's count has tens of thousands of words. It stayed small until the mid-1990s, when stories in the New York Times and elsewhere brought attention, and Talossa moved largely to the web. In April 1996 Madison launched a website for an association of such projects, the League of Secessionist States, which became the most prominent online group of its kind from 1997 to at least 2000. As such, Talossa is an early example of an online community that treats itself as a state. It claims part of Milwaukee as a Greater Talossan Area, and no sovereign state or the UN recognises that claim. As of 5 August 2023 it reported 157 active citizens. It has lasted more than 46 years without seeking anything enforceable from a government.
mechanism: A micronation that asks nothing from any state can last for decades, since nobody needs to decide whether its claim is valid.
